subject: physics
question_text: Explain the terms average velocity and instantaneous velocity. When are they equal?

verification.note: Re-homed from Unit 4 to Unit 3 on 2026-08-22: both source books place this question in Motion in a Straight Line — the Fastrack as Very Short Answer 2 (p.6, 3 stars) and the TSBIE Basic Learning Material as Short Answer 1 (p.4). The two books DISAGREE on the section, so both lengths ship as cuts and the student chooses. The question_id keeps its original mp_ prefix because ids are stable forever. It was asked in the AP March 2026 paper, question 24, which is recorded in appearances[]. Both mark splits are CLAIMS until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms them.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Motion in a Straight Line · 4 marks

steps.label: Average velocity
lines: The ratio of the total displacement to
It does not depend on the path taken
steps.margin_note: Say DISPLACEMENT, not distance. That one word is what makes this velocity and not speed.
steps.why: Average velocity uses only the first and last positions, so the path between them does not enter the calculation — which is exactly why the path does not matter to it.
common_mistakes: Writing distance over time, which defines average speed instead.

recall.must_convey: That average velocity is total displacement over total time.
accept: it does not depend on the path
total displacement ni total time tho
reject: the limit as delta t goes to zero

steps.memory_tip: Average velocity uses only the two END points. The path between them does not matter.

steps.label: Instantaneous velocity
lines: The velocity of the body at one
It is the limit of the average velocity
as the time interval shrinks to zero:
steps.margin_note: Two of the four marks sit here. Write the limit line — the words alone earn one mark, the limit earns the other.
steps.why: Shrinking the interval to nothing turns the average over a stretch into the value at a point — that limit is what a speedometer needle reads.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the limit and writing only dr/dt.
Saying "very small time" instead of the limit as Δt approaches zero.

recall.must_convey: That instantaneous velocity is the limit of delta r by delta t as delta t goes to zero, written dr/dt.
accept: the limit as delta t tends to zero
reject: they are equal in uniform motion

steps.memory_tip: Instantaneous is the SAME ratio with the interval shrunk to zero — that is what d r by d t means.

steps.label: When equal
lines: When the body moves with uniform
looks the same as the whole journey:
steps.margin_note: Uniform VELOCITY, not just uniform speed — the direction must also stay fixed.
steps.why: If the velocity never changes, the average over any stretch is that same unchanging value, so the two definitions stop being different.
common_mistakes: Answering "uniform speed" — a body circling at constant speed still changes direction, so they differ.

recall.must_convey: That they are equal for motion with uniform velocity.
accept: constant speed in a straight line
reject: the limit as delta t goes to zero

steps.memory_tip: They agree only when the velocity never changes. One steady direction, one steady speed.
